title: Sashiko: Lessons from building an agentic code review system for Linux
content:
Sashiko: Lessons from building an agentic code review system for Linux
Roman Gushchin
Software Engineer, AI & Infrastructure
Eric Brewer
VP, Infrastructure & Google Fellow, AI & Infrastructure
The speed of development in large open-source projects has always been limited by code review, not code generation. Even as coding agents get better at writing code, they do not accelerate development on their own. This is especially true of patches to the Linux kernel. Without a way to build trust in proposed changes, more generated code simply piles up in front of the same small group of human maintainers. Some of those patches are solid changes, just written faster; many others are plausible-looking "AI slop" sent by contributors who do not fully understand the systems they are modifying. And the influx of AI-generated security reports, many of which are duplicates or inaccurate, only adds to maintainers’ load.
Linux runs billions of Android phones, most cloud providers, and nearly every supercomputer. It spans more than 35 million lines of code, and over 85,000 changes land every year. Automated build bots and fuzzers like Syzkaller catch build errors and crashes, but code review has always been the main way to guarantee the stability and safety of the kernel. Every day, maintainers read hundreds and hundreds of proposed patches by hand to catch memory leaks, deadlocks, race conditions, and security bugs.
To help maintainers handle the load and catch bugs before they land, the Google AI & Infrastructure team built Sashiko, an open-source, agentic code review system powered by Gemini. We named the project after the Japanese word 刺し子, a stitching technique for artistically reinforcing worn cloth, and donated it to the Linux Foundation earlier this year.
In this blog, we cover the problem Sashiko was designed to solve, how it works, what the data shows, and what we learned from building and running it in the wild.
Reviewing code is hard
Reviewing a change in a complex code base is objectively hard, both for humans and LLMs. It often requires a deep understanding of how the system works in general, well outside the proposed change. In fact, it’s pretty common to see patches that engineers claim perfectly solve the problem, but if they were to be merged, would actually introduce even worse problems (albeit subtle). Traditionally, only experienced maintainers have been able to spot and prevent these issues. The same is true for agentically generated code.
To verify the correctness of a change, a potentially large number of invariants should be proven, which is often a much larger and harder task than developing the change itself. This is true for both human and agentic reviewers. However, LLM-based reviewers have some unique properties, both positive and negative:
- LLMs often struggle to put in enough effort. LLMs are trained to achieve the goal of spending fewer tokens. So they often tend to cut corners and dismiss concerns without proper investigation or flag false positives without proper due diligence.
- LLMs are easier to bias. The current generation of LLMs usually performs much better if provided a single relatively simple task (e.g., prove the patch for memory leaks) rather than multiple tasks (e.g., explore several complex, varied concerns). It’s pretty common for an LLM to find an obvious issue in the code and refuse to look deeper for other types of issues. Also, commit log text can sometimes affect the result of code review in a non-predicatable or even malicious way.
- LLMs don’t have persistent memory. Surprisingly, this is a positive thing for code review: An LLM can review the same or similar patch multiple times as if it were a new patch. No sane human can review the same patch applied to 100 slightly different branches to find the few that have incompatible changes.
How Sashiko reviews a patch
To avoid these failure modes, Sashiko separates finding candidate bugs from verification of those bugs, and requires each pass to record what it ruled out:
Notes on each step:
- Gather context and plan: Sashiko first pulls in the code around the diff (modified functions, struct definitions, and direct callers) and loads the subsystem's domain guides, so the changed lines are never judged in isolation. A planner then decides which specialist passes are needed (skipping hardware checks on pure software code, for example) and sets a reasoning budget for each pass based on patch complexity.
- Parallel specialist sessions: Up to seven specialist sessions run in parallel, each focused on a single class of problems: commit intent, implementation match, control flow, resource lifetimes, locking, security, and hardware. Giving each pass a single focus prevents one type of bug from crowding out another. Each session searches and reads the repository with git tools (averaging about 100 tool calls per review) and outputs two lists: concerns it believes are real, and candidate concerns it investigated and ruled out, along with the code that supports that conclusion.
- Triage: A lead verifier audits those two lists together. Clear-cut bugs already proven by the code in front of it pass straight through; dismissals proven by a local check are dropped. Everything else deserves additional investigation. Crucially, that includes not only contested bugs where specialists disagreed, but also shaky self-dismissals — cases where a specialist spotted a real bug and dismissed it by assuming, without proof, that some unseen caller or lock would prevent it.
- Per-bug deep checks: Instead of checking all difficult cases in one shared prompt, Sashiko gives each difficult case its own verification agent that runs in parallel. Each agent gets one specific question to answer with git tools under a symmetrical rule: Neither a bug claim nor a dismissal is accepted without concrete code proof across all call sites. If a specialist talks itself out of a real bug based on a false assumption, this step catches it and promotes it back to a real finding.
- Review report: Sashiko generates a report that sounds like a human maintainer asking questions about the proposed change, matching the style expected on a Linux mailing list.
All this happens at no cost for developers. Deep agentic reviews at scale require a substantial token budget. If developers had to pay for them with their own API keys, many important contributors would be pushed away. Instead, Sashiko reviews patches sent to public Linux kernel mailing lists, and Google runs the service at sashiko.dev. Everything runs in the open: every prompt, tool call, reasoning step, and ruled-out bug is public. The project initially used the open-source Linux review prompts started by Chris Mason, and more than 100 contributors, including prominent kernel maintainers and engineers, have since helped to improve prompts and Sashiko itself. Recently, Sashiko switched to a different prompt system that combines per-tree or per-version auto-generated notes on code with subjective maintainers notes, which contain directions and instructions from maintainers that can’t be derived from the code.
What the data shows
The real test of an automated reviewer is whether maintainers pay attention to the reports it sends out, and whether those reports track actual software quality. Seven months of Sashiko production data from the kernel mailing lists give a clear picture of both these questions.
It is part of the daily workflow. Sashiko completes roughly 1200 reviews a day across over 100 kernel mailing lists. It sends review emails only to lists whose maintainers opt in, and already over 70 of them have done so. Developers also engage directly with the reports: More than 1500 kernel developers have replied on the mailing lists, and their pushback on false alarms has directly driven improvements to Sashiko's prompts and verification engine. report.summary: Google's open-source Sashiko uses Gemini agents to review Linux kernel patches, separating bug-finding from verification, and now runs ~1,200 reviews a day on kernel mailing lists.
report.background: The Linux kernel spans more than 35 million lines of code and absorbs over 85,000 changes a year, all gated by a relatively small group of human maintainers. Review, not code generation, has always been the real bottleneck: build bots and fuzzers like Syzkaller catch crashes, but only careful reading catches race conditions, deadlocks, memory leaks and subtle security bugs. Faster AI coding agents now pour more patches, plausible-looking "AI slop" and duplicated security reports into the same queue. Google's AI & Infrastructure team built Sashiko (Japanese for a reinforcing stitch), powered by Gemini, to help maintainers triage this load. The project is open source, was donated to the Linux Foundation, and runs as a free public service at sashiko.dev reviewing patches sent to public kernel mailing lists.
key_points: LLM reviewers have known failure modes: they are trained to spend fewer tokens, so they cut corners and dismiss concerns without proof; they perform better on one narrow task than many; and their results can be swayed by commit-log text. But their lack of persistent memory is an advantage, letting them re-review near-identical patches across many branches.

Sashiko first gathers context (surrounding functions, structs, callers, subsystem guides), then a planner picks specialist passes and sets a reasoning budget. Up to seven specialist sessions run in parallel, each focused on one risk class — commit intent, implementation match, control flow, resource lifetimes, locking, security and hardware — averaging about 100 git tool calls per review.

Each specialist returns two lists: concerns it believes are real, and concerns it investigated and ruled out, backed by code. A lead verifier audits both. Shaky self-dismissals — a real bug waved away by assuming an unseen caller or lock would prevent it — are escalated rather than dropped, which is where many misses would otherwise occur.

Every difficult case gets its own verification agent, run in parallel, under a symmetrical rule: neither a bug claim nor a dismissal is accepted without concrete code proof across all call sites. The output is a report written like a human maintainer asking questions, matching Linux mailing list conventions.

Adoption data from seven months in production: roughly 1,200 reviews a day across 100+ lists, with 70+ maintainers opted in; 1,500+ kernel developers have replied, and their pushback on false positives has directly improved prompts and the verification engine. The project has drawn 100+ contributors and recently moved to auto-generated per-tree notes plus maintainer-written guidance.
report.impact: Sashiko's most important lesson is architectural rather than model-centric: separating cheap, broad bug-finding from expensive, adversarial verification beats asking one prompt to do everything. That pattern — parallel focused reviewers, explicit rule-outs, proof required in both directions — is directly reusable by any team building agents over large codebases, and it argues against single-shot "review my diff" prompts. Its fully public reasoning traces also set a transparency bar for AI tooling in critical infrastructure. For the kernel, the effect is triage relief: filtering noise before maintainers spend attention. For ordinary users, the payoff is indirect but real — more scrutiny of patches touching billions of Android devices, cloud servers and supercomputers. The open questions are cost at scale, prompt injection through commit messages, and whether reports stay trusted as AI-generated patch volume grows.
report.tools: Watch Sashiko itself: open source and free at sashiko.dev, with all prompts, tool calls and rule-outs public — a good reference implementation for agentic review. Gemini models power it. Syzkaller remains the complementary fuzzing layer. The Linux kernel mailing list archives and LWN.net coverage show real review threads and maintainer feedback. Chris Mason's original open-source Linux review prompts are worth reading as a starting point, and the Linux Foundation now hosts the project for governance and contribution.
